findings.finding: Child 48f0's sizing basis contradicts the parent's discharged AC6: 48f0 sizes mcp's mem_limit on a '0.97 GB quiet baseline' and a 4.64 GB max / 8.31 GB sum, but the epic's AC6 discharge states there is NO ~0.97 GB quiet baseline (mcp is 2.2-2.9 GiB) and that post-2685 per-service-plus-one-gate sizing sums to 8326 MiB > the 7813 MiB host — rendering 48f0's 6656 MiB mem_limit allocation unsatisfiable.
scenarios: Implementer builds docker-compose.yml to child 48f0's 2048m mcp limit; at the corrected 2.87 GiB steady state mcp exceeds its own limit and OOM-restarts under normal (non-gate) load, i.e. the limit is set below observed steady state — or, honouring the epic's post-2685 sizing, the four limits cannot sum below the host at all.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-derive child 48f0's mem_limit table from the post-2685 measurements and record which of the epic-comment options (A trim gerrit / B ceilings-not-reservations / C resize) the child adopts, since the briefed 6656 MiB allocation no longer matches measured steady state.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile W4 with W1: state whether the memory-aware admission controller is still needed once the batch tier is off-host, and if so specify what it governs (the residual always-up Gerrit+MCP sum is not queueable/refusable like a gate run) and how it enforces on non-admission-gated services — otherwise fold W4's residual role into W2's kernel-enforced mem_limits.
evidence: W4: 'One admission controller aware of total memory, replacing independent gate semaphore + MCP thread limiter + review-bot concurrency, each locally reasonable.'
W1: 'Move gate execution off the Gerrit host … Removes the bursty heavy consumer entirely.'
gate_admission.py:299-340 — current admission is a discrete-run fcntl slot semaphore that FAST-FAILs a gate; it governs queueable runs, not resident always-up services.

Interactive services (Gerrit JVM heap ~2GB pinned, MCP steady 2.87GiB) cannot be 'refused admission' the way a gate can — the plan names them as the residual sum but W4's lever does not apply to them.
findings.finding: W4 ('one admission controller aware of total memory, replacing independent gate semaphore + MCP thread limiter + review-bot concurrency') is not reconciled with W1 (remove the batch gate tier from the host). If W1 lands, the gate semaphore is moot on this host and the residual co-resident load is two ALWAYS-UP interactive services (Gerrit, MCP); admission control — which today (gate_admission.py) is a count-based fcntl slot semaphore over discrete, queueable gate RUNS — has no mechanical analogue for refusing/queueing a resident interactive service, so W4's stated mechanism may be inapplicable to exactly the workloads that remain after W1.
scenarios: W1 ships first (leverage order says it should): the gate semaphore that W4 subsumes no longer runs on this host, leaving W4 governing only Gerrit+MCP, which it cannot gate.
An implementer builds a unified memory-aware admission controller and finds it has nothing queueable left to admit/refuse once gates are off-box.

findings.finding: W4 replaces three existing controls (the gate semaphore, the MCP thread limiter, and review-bot concurrency) with a single admission controller, and W2 introduces per-container memory limits that will cause containers to restart on breach — both are behavior changes to running services, but no rollback/back-out or expand-contract sequencing is stated.

findings.suggested_fix: Sequence W4 expand-contract: land the admission controller alongside the existing limiters (fail-open), validate under load, then retire the old limiters; document reverting limit values if a container restart-storms.

findings.checklist_item: State the disposition the admission controller surfaces when it refuses a gate — explicitly retryable/queued (WAIT_AND_RETRY) given gates are 'queueable' — so a refused admission is never surfaced as a permanent failure.
evidence: W4: 'One admission controller aware of total memory, replacing independent gate semaphore + MCP thread limiter + review-bot concurrency'
AC2: 'an admission is refused ... instead of wedging the host'
Gates are described as 'BATCH ... queueable' in 'Three workloads', implying a refused admission should be retryable, but no disposition word is stated

findings.finding: W4's admission controller and AC2 introduce a new failure arm — a refused admission — but the plan never states its disposition: whether a refused gate is retryable/queued (transient) or dropped/failed (permanent).
scenarios: The admission controller refuses a plan-review gate at peak memory; without a stated contract the gate could be silently dropped/failed instead of queued and retried, turning a resource-limit into a lost review
findings.suggested_fix: Add to W4/AC2: 'A refused admission is a retryable/transient disposition — the gate is queued and re-attempted when memory frees, never failed permanently; the MCP thread limiter and review-bot concurrency refusals inherit the same retryable disposition.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Name AC1's enforcer of record — kernel per-container mem_limit (W2) binds always-up Gerrit+MCP, whereas admission control (W4) binds only queueable gate runs — and state which one provably bounds the residual sum after W1.
evidence: AC1: 'something ENFORCES it rather than documenting it.'
W2 converts 'host wedges' into 'one container restarts, loudly' — a kernel mem_limit is an enforcer that applies to resident services.
W4 proposes admission control as the enforcer, but admission control only binds discrete gate runs (gate_admission.py).
findings.finding: AC1 requires that 'something ENFORCES' the sub-RAM sum, but the plan does not name which workstream is the enforcer of record, leaving ambiguity between W2 (kernel mem_limit, an enforcer that binds always-up services) and W4 (an admission controller that binds only queueable runs). Naming the enforcer would settle the W1/W4 tension above.
scenarios: Two workstreams each claim to be the AC1 enforcer with different mechanics; implementer builds both or neither for the residual interactive load.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Justify W4's bespoke total-memory admission controller against established alternatives (W2 per-container mem_limits as a kernel-enforced aggregate bound, cgroup v2 memory accounting / systemd slices, or a batch queue), and state why those cannot satisfy AC1/AC2 — or fold W4 into W2 if they can.
evidence: W4: 'One admission controller aware of total memory, replacing independent gate semaphore + MCP thread limiter + review-bot concurrency, each locally reasonable.'

Absence: no alternative is weighed. W2 already declares per-container mem_limits, which the kernel enforces as an aggregate bound — the plan does not explain why that is insufficient and a custom controller is additionally required.

Prior art retrieved: ScyllaDB reader-concurrency-semaphore (github.com/scylladb/scylladb/blob/master/docs/dev/reader-concurrency-semaphore.md) does memory-aware admission; scalemind.dev/rate-limiting distinguishes concurrency-limiting from byte/quota-based control — the byte-vs-count admission design space is established, not new.

Prior art retrieved: virtua.cloud and orthogonal.info confirm per-container mem_limit + restart policy already converts 'host wedges' into 'one container restarts' — the exact AC2 property, achievable without a bespoke aggregate controller.
findings.finding: W4 proposes a novel bespoke 'admission controller aware of total memory' that replaces three independent working limiters, without considering established prior art that already bounds aggregate memory (its own W2 per-container mem_limits, cgroup v2 memory accounting / systemd slices, or a queue/scheduler), so the novelty is unjustified against the anti-repackaging / Rule-of-Three test.
findings.location: Workstreams — W4 ("Bound the SUM, not the parts") and AC1
scenarios: W4 is built as new code and duplicates the aggregate-bounding that W2's kernel-enforced mem_limits already provide, adding a maintained component with no marginal safety.
Reviewers cannot tell whether W4 is load-bearing for AC1 or redundant with W2, so AC1 ('something ENFORCES it') may be satisfiable by W2 alone.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short prior-art paragraph under W4: (1) note that W2's summed per-container mem_limits already enforce an aggregate bound at the kernel, satisfying AC1's 'enforces it' for the interactive tier; (2) cite the memory-aware-admission prior art (e.g. ScyllaDB reader-concurrency-semaphore, byte-based limiters) and explain what a unified controller buys beyond per-container limits + W1's tier separation; (3) if the marginal benefit is only queueing/backpressure for gates, scope W4 to that and drop the 'replace all three limiters' framing.
